newsitem.title: CHINA: Shanghai leads China in credit card usage.
newsitem.headline: Shanghai leads China in credit card usage.

text.p: In China, where a preference for bank notes has long held the cashless society at bay, credit cards are gaining popularity, and Shanghai, the country's mercantile hub, is leading the pack, bankers said on Thursday.
"Shanghai is leading China in setting up a cashless payment network and has made rapid progress this year," said an official with the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China (ICBC).
Shanghai had a total of 12 million debit cards, credit cards and chip cards on issue by the end of 1996, official figures show.
That made up 40 percent of the 30 million debit, credit and chip cards on issue for all of China by the end of 1996.
Last year, transactions settled by credit cards accounted for five to eight percent of Shanghai's total retail sales value, the Shanghai-based Business News has reported.

While China's cash-only mentality was changing, most Shanghainese still had limited opportunities to use their plastic because many stores preferred cash to avoid paying commission to banks, analysts said.

China's banks usually charged one to four percent commission based on the total transaction value, but to encourage more people to pay with plastic, some banks now charged less than one percent, analysts said.
Even retailers with point of sale (POS) capabilities, which allows the immediate clearing of a credit card transaction, were sometimes loathe to accept the cards, one local banker said.
By the end of June, of Shanghai's tens of thousands of retail outlets and restaurants, only 800 accepted POS cards, official figures show.

Most payment cards in China were debit cards, requiring money to be first deposited in a bank account, rather than traditional credit cards, which allowed the issuing bank to provide payment, the analyst sources said.
Chip cards, which carry a computer chip for use as stored value cards, were still not widespread, they said.
"It will take another five or more years to change the thinking of local people, and then the card business will really start to flourish," a banker said.
Shanghai was one of 12 cities participating in the Golden Card project, which links all the automatic teller machines (ATMs) in each city to make banking more convenient, bankers and officials said.
Foreign credit card companies, such as Visa and Mastercard, have rushed to connect to the network in a bid to link Shanghai with the rest of the world.

Some 1,128 of Shanghai's ATMs, or more than 70 percent of the city's total, had already been linked to the unified network, with all 10 of the financial institutions with the right to issue payment cards participating, analysts said.
The network would connect all Shanghai's ATMs by the end of 1997, allowing access by a variety of payment cards, they said.
"We now have 420 ATMs linked to the city's unified payment network, compared with 380 at the beginning of this year," said the official of ICBC, which has the most ATMS in Shanghai.
Visa and Mastercard have already said they have linked into the Golden Card project.
"Foreign companies have more experience and advanced technology, which will help us accelerate our local credit card business and lead us into the world market," a local banker said.
